claims.claim: The typical leader TVC has a wide leading edge with lamellipodia-like protrusions that depend on Rhod/f- and Cdc42-controlled actin networks.
claims.source: The predicted leader-dominated protrusive activity of the cell pair was consistent with previous observations that the typical leader TVC has a wide leading edge with lamellipodia-like protrusions that depend on Rhod/f- and Cdc42-controlled actin networks (Christiaen et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Experimentally increasing protrusive activity in one or both migrating cells disrupted their collective polarity, with cells more likely to migrate in parallel.
claims.source: Under these conditions, experimentally increasing protrusive activity in one or both migrating cells disrupted their collective polarity, with cells more likely to migrate in parallel as predicted by in silico simulations (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E that matches computational predictions.

claims.claim: Protrusive activity is suppressed in trailer cells compared to leader and single cells.
claims.source: This result suggests that the protrusive activity is suppressed in trailer cells compared to leader and single cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined computational and experimental results.

claims.claim: Simulations that reduce protrusive activity in the trailer without increasing its retractile forces cause the leader to detach and move forward on its own.
claims.source: Nevertheless, simulations that reduce protrusive activity in the trailer without increasing its retractile forces cause the leader to detach and move forward on its own, overcoming significant mutual adhesion between the two cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Some protrusive activity in the trailer is still required for paired TVC migration.
claims.source: This suggests that some protrusive activity in the trailer is still required, and that, in paired TVCs, the cells exert equivalent forces, while coordinating their activities to distribute protrusive and retractile forces to the leader and trailer cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from computational simulations.

claims.claim: The best computational recapitulation of observed shapes was achieved with centripetal retractive forces dominating in the trailer and centrifugal protrusive forces in the leader.
claims.source: Next, we sought to further probe the supracellular model using phenomenological observations. Notably, the best computational recapitulation of observed shapes was achieved with centripetal retractive forces dominating in the trailer, pulling the cell rear forward and down, while the centrifugal protrusive forces in the leader pushed the front forward (Figure 1B and D, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 1B and D.

claims.claim: iMyo-GFP accumulates at the rear of the trailer cell and is relatively depleted from the leader-trailer junction.
claims.source: Consistent with the model's prediction of a trailer-polarized retractile activity, we observe that iMyo-GFP, an intrabody that recognizes non-muscle myosin II through a conserved epitope (Chaigne et al., 2013; Hashimoto et al., 2015), accumulates at the rear of the trailer cell and is relatively depleted from the leader-trailer junction (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), implying that the retraction in the trailer is dominant, while the retractive force in the leader is weak, lending further support to the hypothesis that TVC pairs migrate as a supracellular collective.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citations to previous work on the iMyo-GFP marker.

claims.claim: Pairs of multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors migrate as a polarized supracellular collective, with protrusive activity and myosin-based retraction distributed across leader and trailer cells, respectively.
claims.source: Taken together, our computational predictions and experimental observations support a model where pairs of multipotent cardiopharyngeal progenitors migrate as a polarized supracellular collective, with protrusive activity and myosin-based retraction distributed across leader and trailer cells, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined computational and experimental findings.

claims.claim: Cell-matrix interactions and distribution of protrusive activity to the leading TVC result in the generation of a broad leading edge during the establishment of collective TVC polarity.
claims.source: Cell-matrix interactions and distribution of protrusive activity to the leading TVC result in the generation of a broad leading edge during the establishment of collective TVC polarity (Bernadskaya et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Conditions that perturb cell-matrix adhesion often increase the sphericity of leading cells, suggesting that they fail to establish flattened protrusions at the leading edge.
claims.source: Conditions that perturb cell-matrix adhesion often increase the sphericity of leading cells, suggesting that they fail to establish flattened protrusions at the leading edge (Bernadskaya et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: TVCs' sphericities did not differ at stage 19, suggesting that they are born with equivalent shapes.
claims.source: TVCs' sphericities did not differ at stage 19, suggesting that they are born with equivalent shapes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental measurements of cell sphericity at different developmental stages.

claims.claim: Cell sphericities begin to differ significantly during migration, indicating establishment of leader/trailer polarity, adoption of distinct states, and orientation in direction of migration.
claims.source: Cell sphericities begin to differ significantly during migration, indicating establishment of leader/trailer polarity, adoption of distinct states (Figure 2A), and orientation in direction of migration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Collective TVC polarization is abolished by disruption of cell-matrix adhesion by misexpression of a dominant-negative version of the collagen receptor, Discoidin domain receptor (Ddrdn).
claims.source: Collective TVC polarization is abolished by disruption of cell-matrix adhesion by misexpression of a dominant-negative version of the collagen receptor, Discoidin domain receptor (Ddrdn), which alters integrin-mediated cell-matrix adhesion and disrupts polarized Bmp-Smad signaling (Bernadskaya et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In simulations, the cell with reduced adhesion was more likely to assume the trailer position.
claims.source: In these conditions, the cell with reduced adhesion was more likely to assume the trailer position (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Coexpression of Intß1dn increased the proportion of labeled trailer cells to 57% in mosaic embryos.
claims.source: In contrast, coexpression of Intß1dn increased the proportion of labeled trailer cells to 57% in mosaic embryos (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Cells that inherited Ddrdn were significantly more likely to be in the trailer position, increasing the proportion of mCherry-labeled cells in the trailer position to 66%.
claims.source: Cells that inherited Ddrdn were significantly more likely to be in the trailer position, increasing the proportion of mCherry-labeled cells in the trailer position to 66% (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Mosaic expression of RhoDFca has the opposite, albeit not statistically significant, effect, promoting positioning of the labeled cell anteriorly.
claims.source: Mosaic expression of RhoDFca has the opposite, albeit not statistically significant, effect, promoting positioning of the labeled cell anteriorly (Figure 2C), further lending support to our hypothesis of leader cells being more protrusive and less retractive than trailers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Reduced cell-matrix adhesion promotes positioning of the cell with reduced adhesion posterior to the cell with more adhesion, thereby preferentially adopting the trailer state.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations indicate that reduced cell-matrix adhesion promotes positioning of the cell with reduced adhesion posterior to the cell with more adhesion, thereby preferentially adopting the trailer state, which in turn suggests that cell-matrix adhesion is stronger in leader cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined computational and experimental results.

claims.claim: Leader cells consistently contained more ventral Lifeact::GFP+ F-actin puncta than trailer cells.
claims.source: Quantifications indicated that leader cells consistently contained more ventral Lifeact::GFP+ F-actin puncta than trailer cells, supporting the prediction that F-actin-rich adhesion complexes are enriched in leading cells during TVC migration (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Increased cell-matrix adhesion and protrusive activity are hallmarks of the leader cell state during collective cell migration.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that increased cell-matrix adhesion and protrusive activity are hallmarks of the leader cell state during collective cell migration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The two cells are not arranged in a linear leader-trailer orientation at birth.
claims.source: However, the two cells are not arranged in a linear leader-trailer orientation at birth (Figure 3A), and previous observations indicated that either cell can assume a leader position, although single-cell lineage tracing indicates that the leader emerges from the most anterior cell in ~95% of embryos (Gline et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Single-cell lineage tracing indicates that the leader emerges from the most anterior cell in ~95% of embryos.
claims.source: However, the two cells are not arranged in a linear leader-trailer orientation at birth (Figure 3A), and previous observations indicated that either cell can assume a leader position, although single-cell lineage tracing indicates that the leader emerges from the most anterior cell in ~95% of embryos (Gline et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Prior to migration at embryonic stage 17, the leader/trailer axis is more orthogonal to the future direction of anterior movement.
claims.source: Tracking cos(θ) to quantify the alignment of cell pairs with direction of migration, with θ defined as the angle between the leader-trailer axis (axis connecting their centers of mass) and the direction of migration (Figure 3A and B), shows that prior to migration at embryonic stage 17 (8.5 hr post fertilization [hpf]), the leader/trailer axis is more orthogonal to the future direction of anterior movement.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: The cells reach their full polarization and alignment with direction of migration by stage 21, a process that takes approximately 1.5 hr at 18°C.
claims.source: The cells reach their full polarization and alignment with direction of migration by stage 21, a process that takes approximately 1.5 hr at 18°C, after which they continue to migrate as a fully polarized cell pair for approximately 2 hr (Figure 3A and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and C.

claims.claim: Either the faster-slower or leader-trailer mode led cells to rearrange into a single file aligned with the migration path.
claims.source: By contrast, either the faster-slower or leader-trailer mode led cells to rearrange into a single file aligned with the migration path (i.e., cos(θ) = 1), with the leader-trailer mode allowing faster alignment, with a half-time to alignment reduced compared to the fast-slower mode (Figure 3D, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3D and Video 4.

claims.claim: The leader-trailer mode allows faster alignment compared to the faster-slower mode.
claims.source: By contrast, either the faster-slower or leader-trailer mode led cells to rearrange into a single file aligned with the migration path (i.e., cos(θ) = 1), with the leader-trailer mode allowing faster alignment, with a half-time to alignment reduced compared to the fast-slower mode (Figure 3D, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3D and Video 4.

claims.claim: In three-cell simulations with the independent mode, cells failed to produce linear arrangements and remained in triangular formation.
claims.source: Similar to two-cell simulations, the independent mode failed to produce linear arrangements and the cells remained in triangular formation with no leader emerging, potentially due to the three-cell system minimizing the adhesive energy when each cell maintains contacts with the other two (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The leader-middle-trailer mode was the most effective at producing full polarization and linear order rapidly in three-cell simulations.
claims.source: The leader-middle-trailer mode was again the most effective at producing full polarization and linear order rapidly (Figure 3E, Video 6), suggesting that basic hierarchical rules of collective polarization can produce linear arrangements of cell groups containing variable numbers of cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3E and Video 6.

claims.claim: In conditions with ectopic FGF/M-Ras/Mek-driven induction, the cells align in the direction of movement in 57% of the experimental embryos.
claims.source: In conditions such as misexpression of a constitutively active form of M-Ras using the Mesp enhancer (Razy-Krajka et al., 2018) (Mesp>M-Rasca), the cells align in the direction of movement in 57% of the experimental embryos, with a single anterior leader, followed by two (13%) or three (87%) cells arranged in a single line (68%, n = 31) (Figure 3F, Videos 7 and 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Videos 7 and 8, with a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Increasing or decreasing cell-cell adhesion energy causes the cell-cell boundary area to increase or decrease, respectively.
claims.source: Multiple simulations varying the cell-cell adhesion energy in our basic model show that cell-cell adhesion strength does not affect the total displacement of cell pairs over long time intervals (Figure 3G, bottom right). However, increasing or decreasing cell-cell adhesion energy causes the cell-cell boundary area to increase or decrease, respectively (Figure 3G, top right, blue plot), which leads to a drastic misalignment of cells with the direction of migration beyond a cell-cell adhesion strength of 10 (relative energy units).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Cells with high cell-cell adhesion will reorient their supracellular polarity away from the direction of migration.
claims.source: This suggests that the extent of cell-cell adhesion may be regulated in vivo and that cells with high cell-cell adhesion will reorient their supracellular polarity away from the direction of migration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from computational simulations.

claims.claim: TVCs move at ~0.4 µm/min, which is relatively slow compared to specialized motile cells.
claims.source: Unlike specialized motile cells, such as Dictyostelium, fish keratocytes, or neutrophils, which can migrate at ~10 µm/min, 7.5 μm/min, and ~19 μm/min, respectively (Buenemann et al., 2010; Graham et al., 2013; Hoang et al., 2013), TVCs move at ~0.4 µm/min, which is relatively slow, but not unexpected for a developmental migration that contributes to the establishment of accurate cellular patterns in the embryo (Trepat et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on cell migration speeds.

claims.claim: In simulations, motile cell pairs are always more persistent than single cells when centers of mass are tracked over time.
claims.source: In simulations, motile cell pairs are always more persistent than single cells when centers of mass are tracked over time for each condition, suggesting that single cells are more sensitive to directional stochasticity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations.

claims.claim: The total length of the migration path in the simulations was not altered, suggesting that the decreased displacement is a function of the meandering path traveled by the less persistent single cells.
claims.source: Of note, the total length of the migration path in the simulations was not altered, suggesting that the decreased displacement is a function of the meandering path traveled by the less persistent single cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from computational simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In agreement with simulations, TVC pairs migrated further from the anterior ATM than single cells in vivo.
claims.source: We compared the final displacement of single TVCs in vivo to the total displacement of the leader TVC. In agreement with simulations, TVC pairs migrated further from the anterior ATM than single cells (Gline et al., 2015; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In control conditions, the leader and trailer migrate with similar persistence.
claims.source: In control conditions, the leader and trailer migrate with similar persistence; however, the migration paths of single TVCs were significantly less persistent than those of either leader or trailer cells, suggesting that in vivo, collective organization confers robust directionality to the migrating cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: The migration paths of single TVCs were significantly less persistent than those of either leader or trailer cells.
claims.source: In control conditions, the leader and trailer migrate with similar persistence; however, the migration paths of single TVCs were significantly less persistent than those of either leader or trailer cells, suggesting that in vivo, collective organization confers robust directionality to the migrating cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: Collective organization confers robust directionality to the migrating cells in vivo.
claims.source: In control conditions, the leader and trailer migrate with similar persistence; however, the migration paths of single TVCs were significantly less persistent than those of either leader or trailer cells, suggesting that in vivo, collective organization confers robust directionality to the migrating cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations.

claims.claim: Both simulations and in vivo observations suggested that polarized cell pairs migrate with increased robustness to fluctuations in directionality compared to single cells.
claims.source: In summary, both simulations and in vivo observations suggested that polarized cell pairs migrate with increased robustness to fluctuations in directionality compared to single cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined computational and experimental findings.

claims.claim: Shortly after the onset of migration, the TVCs penetrate the extracellular space between the ventral trunk epidermis and the softer trunk endoderm, which locally deforms as TVCs progress anteriorly.
claims.source: Specifically, shortly after the onset of migration, the TVCs penetrate the extracellular space between the ventral trunk epidermis, which they use as stiff substrate, and the softer trunk endoderm, which locally deforms as TVCs progress anteriorly (Gline et al., 2015; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5A and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The trunk endoderm likely exerts mechanical resistance to the passage of the TVCs.
claims.source: We reasoned that the trunk endoderm likely exerts mechanical resistance to the passage of the TVCs and hypothesized that this resistance may be better overcome by polarized cell pairs (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations and reasoning.

claims.claim: When two cells migrate in a leader-trailer arrangement, the surface that the leader exposes to mechanical resistance is equivalent to that of a single cell, while the trailer pushes from the rear, therefore adding forward-bearing compression force to overcome endoderm resistance.
claims.source: We predicted that when two cells migrate in a leader-trailer arrangement, the surface that the leader exposes to mechanical resistance is equivalent to that of a single cell, while the trailer pushes from the rear, therefore adding forward-bearing compression force to overcome endoderm resistance (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on reasoning and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: When modeling a softer endoderm, polarized cell pairs perform best, whether in supracellular mode or equivalent force distribution, while side-by-side cells were the slowest.
claims.source: When modeling a softer endoderm, by modulating volume preservation and cortical tension parameters relative to those of the TVCs (see Appendix 1), polarized cell pairs perform best, whether in supracellular mode or equivalent force distribution, while side-by-side cells were the slowest, presumably because they expose a greater surface to mechanical resistance (Figure 5B and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 5B and D.

claims.claim: Two equivalent cells moving in single file advanced marginally faster than the supracellular pair when modeling a softer endoderm.
claims.source: Notably, two equivalent cells moving in single file advanced marginally faster than the supracellular pair, suggesting that cell alignment itself is a key determinant of efficient migration under the soft tissue.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations.

claims.claim: When simulating a stiffer endoderm, the advantage of supracellular organization became more apparent, with the supracellular collective migrating faster than other arrangements.
claims.source: When simulating a stiffer endoderm, the advantage of supracellular organization became more apparent. In these simulations, the supracellular collective migrated faster than other arrangements (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Cells migrating side-by-side were slower than single cells with either endoderm stiffness.
claims.source: Notably, cells migrating side-by-side were slower than single cells with either endoderm stiffness (Figure 5D), which is consistent with the notion that a more extended surface of contact with the endoderm exposes them to greater mechanical resistance, while the smooth teardrop shape of single cells may be near optimal for lowering the resistive deformations of the endoderm.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The collective shape resulting from supracellular organization optimally minimizes mechanical resistance of the surrounding tissue to migration.
claims.source: This suggests that the collective shape resulting from supracellular organization optimally minimizes mechanical resistance of the surrounding tissue to migration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from computational simulations.

claims.claim: In vivo, the interactions between TVCs and endoderm cells are likely more complex, involving indirect cell-cell signaling via extracellular deposition of collagen9-a1 by the endoderm.
claims.source: The predicted relative speeds of cells migrating under the endoderm are based on the simplest model, which assumes that the endoderm's primary effect is mechanical resistance to deformation. In vivo, the interactions between TVCs and endoderm cells are likely more complex, involving indirect cell-cell signaling via extracellular deposition of collagen9-a1 by the endoderm (Bernadskaya et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The collective organization of migrating cardiopharyngeal progenitors allows them to overcome mechanical resistance from the deforming endoderm and reach a typically mesodermal position between germ layers for cardiac organogenesis.
claims.source: In summary, the combined in silico simulations and in vivo observations indicate that the collective organization of migrating cardiopharyngeal progenitors allows them to overcome mechanical resistance from the deforming endoderm and reach a typically mesodermal position between germ layers for cardiac organogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined computational and experimental findings.

claims.source: Instead, we surmise that this 'rear-wheel' drive represents a back-to-front mechanical input, which propagates as compression force and emerges from rear-localized myosin activity, possibly in response to chemorepulsive inputs integrated by the trailer.

results.result: Ciona cardiopharyngeal progenitors migrate as a supracellular collective with polarized distribution of protrusive forces, cell-matrix adhesion, and myosin-based retraction forces along the leader-trailer axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C11, C14-C15, C24-C26 collectively establish that TVC pairs migrate as a supracellular collective with differential force distributions. The computational modeling (C14-C15, C24) predicts centripetal retraction in the trailer and centrifugal protrusion in the leader, which is validated by experimental observations of myosin distribution (C25) and cell morphology (C10-C11). The convergence of computational predictions and experimental data provides strong support for this core finding.

results.result: Cell-matrix adhesion is polarized to the leader cell and is necessary for establishing and maintaining collective polarity during TVC migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C38 demonstrate through both computational simulations (C32) and experimental perturbations (C33-C35) that reduced cell-matrix adhesion biases cells toward the trailer position. The experimental data showing enrichment of F-actin puncta in leader cells (C37) and the temporal establishment of sphericity differences (C29-C30) provide converging evidence. The statistical significance reported for mosaic perturbations (C33-C34) strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: A hierarchical leader-trailer mode of cell-cell communication establishes collective polarity aligned with the direction of migration more efficiently than alternative modes.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42, C44-C48 show that cells are not initially aligned (C39, C41) but progressively polarize (C42). Computational simulations (C44-C47) predict that a leader-trailer mode produces faster alignment than faster-slower or independent modes, which is validated by experimental observations of 3-4 cell groups following ectopic induction (C48). The agreement between simulation predictions and experimental observations supports this mechanism.

results.result: Polarized cell pairs exhibit greater persistence and migrate longer distances than single cells due to reduced sensitivity to directional fluctuations.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C51-C58, C98-C99 demonstrate through both simulations (C52-C53) and in vivo observations (C54-C56) that cell pairs are more persistent than single cells. The experimental data showing significantly greater displacement of pairs versus single cells (C54) and reduced persistence of single TVCs (C56) with statistical significance provides strong support. The mechanistic explanation involving buffering of directional noise is well-supported by the combined computational and experimental evidence.

results.result: Supracellular organization allows polarized cell pairs to overcome mechanical resistance from the trunk endoderm more effectively than single cells or side-by-side arrangements.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C59-C66, C68, C104 show through computational simulations that supracellular pairs migrate faster than other arrangements when encountering endodermal resistance, with the advantage increasing with endoderm stiffness (C64). The experimental observation of endodermal deformation (C59) and the systematic comparison of different cell arrangements in simulations (C62-C65) provide strong support. However, the authors acknowledge that in vivo interactions are likely more complex (C67), which is appropriately noted as a limitation.

results.result: Protrusive activity must be suppressed in the trailer cell relative to the leader to maintain collective polarity, but some trailer protrusion is required for paired migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C23 demonstrate through computational modeling (C16-C18, C22) that equivalent protrusive activity disrupts polarity, which is validated experimentally by RhoDFca overexpression (C20). The simulations showing that complete suppression of trailer protrusion causes detachment (C22) support the conclusion that some trailer protrusion is necessary (C23). The convergence of computational predictions and experimental validation provides strong support.

results.result: Cell-cell adhesion strength must be balanced to maintain collective integrity while permitting proper alignment with the migration direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50, C81-C83 show through computational simulations that excessive cell-cell adhesion disrupts alignment with migration direction (C49-C50) while insufficient adhesion causes cell detachment (C81). The model prediction that excessive adhesion antagonizes cell-matrix adhesion (C82) is consistent with known biochemical cross-talk (C83). However, this result lacks direct experimental validation in the TVC system, relying primarily on computational predictions and citations to other systems.

results.result: The Cellular Potts Model can recapitulate observed cell shapes and behaviors by modeling mechanical forces at the cellular periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C75-C79 establish the validity of the CPM approach for modeling TVC migration. The model's ability to reproduce observed shapes (C12) and the justification for using CPM based on its computational efficiency (C75) and ability to capture mechanical forces (C76-C79) are well-supported. This methodological result is essential for interpreting the computational predictions throughout the study.

results.result: Supracellular organization requires coordinated 'division of labor' through front-to-back and back-to-front signaling mechanisms that remain to be fully elucidated.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C6, C80, C84-C97, C100-C101, C105 propose mechanisms for coordinating supracellular organization, including rear-wheel drive (C85, C87), suppression of protrusion (C95-C97), and potential roles for PCP signaling (C89-C90). However, most of these claims are speculative (C87-C88, C90, C92-C94, C97, C100) or based on comparisons to other systems (C85-C86, C89, C96). While the need for such mechanisms is well-established by the data, the specific molecular mechanisms remain hypothetical and require future experimental validation.

results.result: Ciona TVCs represent a simple and tractable model system for studying collective cell migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 establish the rationale for using Ciona TVCs as a model system. These claims are supported by citations to previous work (C69, C71) and describe well-established features of the system (C70, C72-C73). This provides appropriate context for the study but represents background knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: TVC-endoderm interactions involve both mechanical resistance and biochemical signaling through collagen9-a1 deposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C102-C103 acknowledge that while the computational model focuses on mechanical resistance, in vivo interactions are more complex and involve collagen9-a1-mediated signaling (C103). This is appropriately cited to previous work (C102-C103) and represents an important caveat to the mechanical modeling. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation (C67).
